When the reward model and policy share the same pretrained base, they inherit identical frequency biases and representational blind spots, which creates a pathological feedback loop: the reward model assigns higher scores to completions that look like what the shared base finds natural, the policy optimizes toward those completions, and rare-token miscalibration is never corrected because the reward signal itself has no independent coverage of those regions — it's blind in exactly the same places the policy is blind. Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) partially mitigates this through the critique-revision loop, where the model is forced to evaluate its own outputs against explicit principles before the preference model is trained, injecting some diversity into the reward signal's coverage — but the critique model still shares the base, so its assessments of rare-token factual claims remain unreliable for the same frequency-bias reasons, and the calibration improvement is largely confined to stylistic and safety dimensions rather than factual token probability. In contrast, independently trained reward models — particularly those trained on different corpora or architectures — introduce coverage heterogeneity: the reward model may have stronger signal on rare tokens in domains where the policy base is weak, and disagreement between reward model confidence and policy confidence creates gradient pressure that can actually push rare-token logits toward better calibration, though this benefit is noisy and depends heavily on whether the independent reward model's training data overlaps the relevant rare-token distribution. Burns et al. (2023, "Weak-to-Strong Generalization") touch on the related problem that a stronger model supervised by a weaker one inherits the weaker model's blind spots in subtle ways — the analogous dynamic here is that shared-base RLHF means the policy can never exceed the reward model's calibration ceiling on rare tokens, whereas independent reward models at least allow the possibility of orthogonal error, which is recoverable. The practical implication for self-play setups like SPIN (Chen et al., 2024) is that iterative self-improvement may tighten calibration on the high-frequency, high-reward region of token space while simultaneously degrading it on rare tokens across iterations, because each round of self-play further concentrates gradient signal where the model already has coverage and further starves the long tail — a slow, compounding miscalibration that becomes invisible in aggregate metrics like perplexity or average ECE but is catastrophic for high-stakes rare-token predictions.

Re-training only the unembedding layer is a tempting intervention because it's computationally cheap and targets the most proximal source of logit distortion, but it breaks on a fundamental assumption: the residual stream representations feeding into the unembedding layer have also been distorted by RLHF, meaning the unembedding matrix was trained to map from corrupted internal representations to output tokens, and re-training it on clean calibration data forces it to map from those same corrupted representations to a different output distribution — you're not fixing miscalibration, you're learning a new miscalibrated mapping on top of distorted inputs. The specific failure mode is representation-output misalignment: after RLHF, the residual stream at rare-token positions carries activations that have been shaped by reward-driven attention patterns throughout the network, so the geometric structure of the final hidden state is no longer the same as it was during pretraining when the original unembedding matrix was meaningful — re-initializing and retraining the unembedding layer on held-out calibration data will find a solution that fits the calibration set but generalizes poorly because the underlying representation geometry is prompt-distribution-dependent in ways the calibration set cannot fully cover. Empirically, this is analogous to the failure mode documented in Zhan et al. and related probing classifier work: linear probes trained on top of fine-tuned representations achieve good in-distribution accuracy but degrade sharply under distribution shift precisely because they're fitting to representation geometry that is itself unstable across prompt distributions. A secondary breakage is that the unembedding matrix in most transformer architectures is weight-tied to the input embedding matrix (Press & Wolf, 2017), so re-training the unembedding layer either requires untying weights — which disrupts the semantic geometry that input embeddings depend on for attention computation throughout the network — or accepting that re-training propagates changes back into input embeddings, cascading distortions through every attention layer that uses those embeddings for key-query computation. The viable partial intervention is not re-training but post-hoc affine correction of the unembedding layer: learning a small affine transform (scaling + rotation) applied to the final residual stream before the unembedding projection, trained on calibration data with a proper scoring rule objective, which can correct the angular distortion without disrupting the weight-tied embedding geometry or requiring the unembedding matrix to generalize across the full corrupted representation manifold — though this still inherits the fundamental limitation that calibration improvements are bounded by how well the affine transform can approximate the true (nonlinear) correction needed.
